Gamma Ray Cameras and Radiography Fundamental and critical technology to DARHT are the GRCs that image the imploding object illuminated by the x-rays from A1 and A2. This is essentially the principal measurement for DARHT. As with others, this capability has evolved and matured over the years, and that general development path establishes much of the basis for DARHT’s future. Table III outlines the proposed development for GRC systems. DARHT’s accelerators produce intense forward-directed x-ray beams via Bremsstrahlung x-ray production. To minimize scattered radiation, the forward-directed beams are collimated and shielded using tungsten and other materials. However, limited physical space around the x-ray source restricts the amount of shielding that can be used. Therefore, a measurable portion of the x-ray beam, outside the acceptance angle of the collimation, will reach the detector plane. This flux travels outside of the direct beamline but can subsequently enter the GRC enclosures through Compton scattering. The Compton-scattered photons may have sufficient residual energy such that they can interfere with the electronics of the GRC CCDs themselves. In an extreme case, with no effective shielding, the gamma rays could damage the CCD electronics of the camera. Stray neutrons are also produced by the powerful DARHT accelerators. The dominant process is photo-neutron production, where a high-energy x-ray interacts with a bound neutron in a typically high-Z material and knocks the neutron out of the nucleus. The neutrons can undergo multiple scattering events and reach the CCD detector. Neutrons can also interfere with the CCD electronics and cause interference, called single event upsets. Both the neutron and gamma ray mechanisms cause “stars” in the radiographic images. Therefore, it is essential to properly shield the GRC systems from both neutron and gamma ray fluxes. The present shielding system at DARHT consists of an engineered system of steel and polyethylene that is 7 in. thick followed by concrete blocks that are 24 in. thick. The total shielding thickness causes significant crowding on the firing point, so a desirable solution would provide equal or better shielding of both gamma and neutron fluxes, but within much less space. This would enable more flexibility for dynamic and static experiment configurations within the firing point WE and is essential for implementation of the MPTL. A preliminary study of GRC shielding was com- pleted in 2021 [Mendez, 2021].
